UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                           BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Columbia Gulf Transmission, LLC                                              Docket No. CP26-25-000


        TENTH SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF JUSTIN KULOVSEK
  AND COMMENTS ON THE AUGUST 11, 2026 ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
 (Request for an Environmental Impact Statement or Supplemental Environmental Assessment
under 18 C.F.R. § 380.6; the Alternatives Baseline; the Record at Milepost 4.25; the Section 401
   Certification and EA Condition 12; Unresolved Consultations; and Requested Conditions)
                                     Filed: September 10, 2026

I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

Justin Kulovsek, an intervenor of record in this proceeding, respectfully submits these Tenth
Supplemental Comments pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and
Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, in response to the Environmental Assessment for the Maysville
Project issued by Commission staff on August 11, 2026 (Accession No. 20260811-3006) (“EA”),
notice of which was published at 91 Fed. Reg. 52685 (Aug. 14, 2026). The Commission granted
Mr. Kulovsek’s motion to intervene on May 19, 2026 (Accession No. 20260519-3015). Mr.
Kulovsek appears pro se. His property at 7350 Flemingsburg Road, Morehead, Kentucky,
comprising applicant tracts KY-RO-043.000 and KY-RO-044.000, lies at approximately Milepost
4.25 of the proposed route. Page references to the EA are to the printed page numbers of the body
of the document.

These comments do not repeat the record Mr. Kulovsek has developed in twelve prior filings, each
of which is incorporated by reference (subject to the correction in Part I.C below): the Motion to
Intervene, Protest, and Comments (Accession No. 20260417-5016); the comments on Kentucky
notification law (Accession No. 20260515-5085); the First through Ninth Supplemental
Comments (Accession Nos. 20260615-5090, 20260623-5089, 20260623-5171, 20260625-5107,
20260708-5031, 20260721-5110, 20260731-5242, 20260803-5245, and 20260805-5027); and the
comments correcting the property-access record (Accession No. 20260713-5093). Mr. Kulovsek




            Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 1
 continues to oppose and protest the proposed alignment where it crosses or directly affects his
property. Nothing in these comments waives that protest or any objection, claim, or property right.

A. The scope of the relief sought

Mr. Kulovsek is aware of Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, 605 U.S. 168
(2025), and of Sierra Club v. FERC, No. 24-1099 (D.C. Cir. Sept. 30, 2025), in which the D.C.
Circuit applied Seven County to a pipeline built to supply a single power plant. Consistent with
those decisions, these comments do not ask the Commission to analyze the environmental effects
of any separate project, including the Spurlock Station co-firing conversion or any prospective
industrial load in Mason County. Where these comments refer to such matters, they do so only for
their bearing on the applicant’s stated purpose and need, on the baseline Commission staff used to
evaluate alternatives, and on the completeness of the Commission’s own record.

B. Summary of the matters addressed

Part II addresses the threshold question the EA never answers: why a 41.96-mile greenfield
interstate pipeline received an environmental assessment when the Commission’s own regulation
provides that an environmental impact statement “will normally be prepared first” for that category
of project. Part III addresses the EA’s admission that its system-alternative comparison was run
against a demand of 140,000 dekatherms per day rather than the 340,000 dekatherms per day for
which certification is sought, and the record evidence bearing on that increase that the EA does
not examine. Part IV addresses the record at Milepost 4.25, including safety tables that predate the
centerline shift the EA adopts, the rejection of Suggested Deviation 6b on grounds the EA concedes
neither the landowner nor Columbia Gulf identified, and recommended Condition 15. Part V
addresses the Kentucky Section 401 certification issued August 4, 2026, which EA Condition 12
would make a mandatory condition of any certificate, which the EA treats as still pending, and
which Columbia Gulf filed on the docket on September 9, 2026, the day before these comments.
Part VI addresses unresolved Endangered Species Act and Section 106 matters, the county
governments’ filed opposition, emergency-response coordination, and public participation. Part
VII identifies documentary errors in the EA. Part VIII addresses schedule. Part IX sets out a narrow
request for hearing procedures, and Part X states the relief requested.




            Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 2
 C. Correction to the Fifth Supplemental Comments regarding KRS 100.289

Mr. Kulovsek’s Fifth Supplemental Comments (Accession No. 20260708-5031), and his May 15,
2026 comments (Accession No. 20260515-5085), characterized Kentucky House Bill 195 (2022),
codified at KRS 100.289, as a landowner-protection statute imposing a duty on natural gas
transmission pipeline operators to notify property owners within 660 feet of a proposed pipeline.
On review of the enrolled bill, the codified statute, and the Legislative Research Commission’s
summary, that characterization is incorrect, and Mr. Kulovsek withdraws it.

The statute’s catchline begins “Notification of pipeline operator about planned development.”
Subsection (3) provides that for a new residential or nonresidential development located within
660 feet of the center point of a natural gas transmission pipeline “that was constructed or operated
prior to the development, the developer shall notify the operator.” The Legislative Research
Commission’s summary states that the bill would “establish notification requirements for
developers that are locating developments within 660 feet of natural gas transmission pipelines”
and “require a notified pipeline operator to provide pipeline location information to the developer.”
Three features of the statute are dispositive against the earlier reading. The duty of notice runs
from developer to operator. The statute applies only where the pipeline “was constructed or
operated prior to the development,” so a proposed pipeline crossing existing properties is outside
it. The enforcement mechanism is a planning commission’s withholding of final plat approval
under subsection (8), a mechanism that could not bind Columbia Gulf. KRS 100.289 is an
encroachment-prevention statute that protects existing pipelines from later development;
subsection (9) preserves Kentucky’s one-call regime. It imposes no duty on Columbia Gulf in this
proceeding.

This correction does not disturb the evidentiary exhibit filed with the Fifth Supplemental, EPIC
Report No. 2026-001, which remains in the record, and no argument in these Tenth Supplemental
Comments relies on KRS 100.289. Mr. Kulovsek submits this correction to keep the record
accurate, consistent with the certification his signature carries under 18 C.F.R. § 385.2005(a)(2).




              Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 3
 II. THE EA DOES NOT EXPLAIN WHY A 41.96-MILE GREENFIELD PIPELINE
RECEIVED AN ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT RATHER THAN AN
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STATEMENT

A. The Commission’s regulation establishes a presumption the EA does not acknowledge

The Commission’s regulations provide that, “[e]xcept as provided in paragraph (b) of this section,
an environmental impact statement will normally be prepared first for” a listed set of projects, the
third of which is “[m]ajor pipeline construction projects under section 7 of the Natural Gas Act
using rights-of-way in which there is no existing natural gas pipeline.” 18 C.F.R. § 380.6(a), (a)(3).
Paragraph (b) supplies the exception: “If the Commission believes that a proposed action identified
in paragraph (a) of this section may not be a major Federal action significantly affecting the quality
of the human environment, an environmental assessment, rather than an environmental impact
statement, will be prepared first.” 18 C.F.R. § 380.6(b). Order No. 908, which removed references
to the rescinded Council on Environmental Quality regulations from Part 380, did not amend §
380.6. 90 Fed. Reg. 29423 (July 3, 2025).

The EA describes the proposed action, in staff’s own words, as “41.96 miles of new 30-inch-
diameter greenfield natural gas pipeline beginning in Rowan County, Kentucky, continuing
through Fleming County, Kentucky, and terminating in Mason County, Kentucky.” EA at 4. The
only route-wide figure in the document bearing on collocation is Appendix H, Table 2, which
reports the “Percent Adjacent to Existing ROW” for the proposed route as 31. EA, App. H at H-2.
Adjacency to an existing right-of-way of any kind is not use of a right-of-way “in which there is
no existing natural gas pipeline,” and the EA never states how many of the 41.96 miles, if any,
share a right-of-way with an existing natural gas pipeline. The EA’s own land-use discussion
describes the existing corridors in the area as “roads, railroads, and associated easements.” EA at
32. On the face of the document, the Project is within § 380.6(a)(3).

The EA does not cite § 380.6. The only reference to Part 380 in the document is a general citation
to “18 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 380” as the source of the Commission’s NEPA
regulations. EA, letter to interested parties, at 1 n.3. The words “environmental impact statement”
do not appear. The staff certification that precedes the table of contents certifies compliance with
the statutory page limit and the statutory deadline; it does not address § 380.6. The document
therefore never acknowledges that an environmental impact statement is the presumptive


             Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 4
 document for this category of project, never states that staff is proceeding under the exception in
paragraph (b), and never gives a reason for doing so.

A regulatory presumption cannot be rebutted by silence. The D.C. Circuit’s test for a finding of no
significant impact asks whether the agency “has accurately identified the relevant environmental
concern,” “has taken a hard look at the problem in preparing its EA,” “is able to make a convincing
case for its finding of no significant impact,” and “has shown that even if there is an impact of true
significance, an EIS is unnecessary because changes or safeguards in the project sufficiently
reduce the impact to a minimum.” Myersville Citizens for a Rural Community, Inc. v. FERC, 783
F.3d 1301, 1322-23 (D.C. Cir. 2015). An EA that does not engage the Commission’s own
presumption in favor of an EIS for this class of project does not make that case.

B. The finding of no significant impact rests on determinations the EA defers to after the
comment period

The EA recommends a finding of no significant impact, EA at 64, while acknowledging that the
determinations on which that finding depends are incomplete. Consultation with the U.S. Fish and
Wildlife Service is “ongoing” for seven federally listed mussel species, Phase 1 mussel surveys
were “to be conducted in the summer of 2026,” and recommended Condition 14 bars construction
until consultation is complete. EA at 28-29, 68. Section 106 compliance “cannot be completed at
this time pending review and concurrence of the mechanical trenching report to determine the
NRHP eligibility of four archaeological sites,” and Table A-3 anticipates receipt of the deep-
testing addendum in November 2026. EA at 10, 42. The Clean Water Act Section 404 verification
is anticipated in September 2026, and the Section 401 certification is listed as anticipated in August
2026. EA at 10. Every one of those results, other than the Section 401 certification (which issued
August 4, 2026 and was filed on the docket on September 9, 2026, one day before the close of
comments, see Part V), will arrive after the September 10, 2026 comment deadline, and none has
been or will be subject to public comment unless the Commission provides for it.

Mr. Kulovsek recognizes that the Commission routinely conditions certificates on completion of
consultation. The point here is narrower. Under 42 U.S.C. § 4336(b)(2), an environmental
assessment is the appropriate document where an action “does not have a reasonably foreseeable
significant effect on the quality of the human environment, or if the significance of such effect is
unknown.” Section 4336(b)(2) permits an environmental assessment where significance is


             Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 5
 unknown; it does not permit a finding of no significant impact while significance remains
unknown. Where the Commission’s own regulation presumes an EIS for this class of project,
where the effects on listed species and historic properties are still being determined, and where the
record shows contested factual issues at specific locations (Parts IV and V below), the choice to
proceed to a finding of no significant impact on an EA requires an explanation. See Sierra Club v.
FERC, 68 F.4th 630 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Commission “inadequately explained its decision not to
prepare a supplemental environmental impact statement” in light of the record before it).

C. Requested action

Mr. Kulovsek requests that the Commission prepare an environmental impact statement in
accordance with 18 C.F.R. § 380.6(a)(3) or, if the Commission concludes that paragraph (b)
applies, that it state on the record the basis for that conclusion and prepare a supplemental
environmental assessment that incorporates the completed Endangered Species Act consultation,
the Section 106 determinations, the Section 404 verification, and the Section 401 certification,
with an opportunity for public comment before any certificate order issues.

III. THE SYSTEM-ALTERNATIVE COMPARISON WAS RUN AGAINST THE
WRONG PURPOSE AND NEED, AND THE EA DOES NOT EXAMINE THE
INCREASE FROM 140,000 TO 340,000 DTH/D

A. The EA admits the error and reasons around it instead of correcting it

NEPA requires consideration of “a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed agency action
... that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal.”
42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C)(iii). Each environmental document must include “a statement of purpose
and need that briefly summarizes the underlying purpose and need for the proposed agency action.”
42 U.S.C. § 4336a(d). The EA states the purpose as delivery of “up to 340,000 dekatherms per day
of firm transportation service to East Kentucky Power Cooperative’s (EKPC’s) upgraded
generation resources at its Hugh L. Spurlock Power Station.” EA at 1.

The EA then states that its system-alternative comparison was not performed against that purpose:

       “While the table depicts most environmental effects as being less than those of the
       alternative, this analysis was done for a demand of 140,000 Dth/d (which was the
       initial project need) instead of the ultimately required 340,000 Dth/d. Therefore,
       this system alternative would require additional looping of the E-system pipeline


            Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 6
        than depicted in the table, which would increase the estimated route length for this
       alternative and corresponding effects to be more in line with the proposed Project.”
       EA at 60.
Appendix H, Table 1, the only quantitative comparison of the system alternative in the record,
carries a footnote to the same effect: the alternative “was developed in response to the former
purpose and need of the Project with a lower capacity. As the Project has since evolved to require
a larger capacity in natural gas transportation, this system alternative is no longer a viable option
for the Project.” EA, App. H at H-1 n.a.

Staff thus acknowledges that the comparison used the wrong demand figure, states that correcting
it would change the results, and then declines to correct it. Staff gives two further reasons: 22
additional residences within 50 feet of the construction right-of-way, and permanent air emissions
from two meter stations and a regulator station. EA at 60. Both were developed for the same
140,000 Dth/d configuration and, like every other row in Appendix H, Table 1, would change with
the looping staff says is required. The table cannot be disclaimed for one purpose and relied on for
another. The conclusion that the alternative “does not present a significant environmental
advantage,” EA at 60, rests on a table whose input assumption staff has disclaimed. An alternatives
analysis “must be bounded by some notion of feasibility,” Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp.
v. NRDC, 435 U.S. 519, 551 (1978), but the feasibility judgment has to be made against the project
actually proposed. The remedy is simple and inexpensive: recalculate Appendix H, Table 1 at
340,000 Dth/d, file the recalculated comparison, and state whether the conclusion changes.

B. The record explains when the need changed, and the EA does not

The EA describes 140,000 Dth/d as “the initial project need” and 340,000 Dth/d as “ultimately
required,” EA at 60, without stating when, why, or on what basis the need more than doubled. The
public record of the Kentucky Public Service Commission supplies the chronology the EA omits.

In Case No. 2025-00321, EKPC applied on October 7, 2025 for authority to incur up to $1 billion
of debt and to enter into precedent agreements with Columbia Gulf for the Spurlock, Cooper, and
Liberty projects. Exhibit 6 to that application contains two EKPC board resolutions. The first,
adopted September 10, 2024, authorized execution of the precedent agreements “prior to
September 30, 2024, at a total estimated cost of $1,577,488,000 over a 20-year term for laterals.”
The second, adopted May 13, 2025, recites that “[t]he Pipeline Expansion Projects are currently



            Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 7
 sized to consist of pipe that is 24″ diameter; however, new information has revealed that 30″
diameter pipe provides long-term flexibility and value,” and authorized “the two (2) individual
Amended and Restated Precedent Agreements for the New Generation Projects at Spurlock and
Cooper, prior to May 15, 2025, upsizing to 30″ diameter pipe, for a combined amended total cost
for the Pipeline Expansion Projects of approximately $1,826,200,000 over a 20-year term.” The
same resolution states that “[t]he incremental capital cost borne by Columbia Gulf of upsizing over
the 20-year term is approximately $20,000,000 or $0.03/Dth for Spurlock,” and that the size
increase “would add approximately $0.300/MWh to the dispatch cost of Spurlock (10,000
BTU/kWh average heat rate) when operating at 50% co-firing of coal and gas.” Paragraph 25 of
the application states that TC Energy “will have an estimated $378,495,290 of capital on the
Maysville Project (Spurlock Station). This will be 30″ diameter pipe on an approximately 42-mile
extension.” The precedent agreements themselves were filed under seal as Exhibit 7; the Kentucky
commission authorized EKPC to execute them by order dated January 29, 2026, and granted
confidential treatment by order dated May 28, 2026. The public excerpts are filed as Exhibit C.
Mr. Kulovsek relies only on the public portions of that record and does not seek access to the
sealed agreements through this Commission.

Two points follow. First, the decision to upsize the Spurlock lateral from 24-inch to 30-inch pipe
was made and board-approved by May 15, 2025, six months before Columbia Gulf filed its
application here on November 17, 2025. The “new information” that drove it is not identified in
any public document Mr. Kulovsek has located, and the EA does not ask what it was. Second, the
same resolution ties the upsizing to a 50 percent co-firing scenario at Spurlock, which is the
maximum co-firing level EKPC described to the Kentucky commission. EKPC’s application in
Case No. 2024-00370 states that “[e]ach unit will be capable of burning up to 50% of fuel gas,”
that the co-firing project “will not increase the units’ total capacity,” and that the co-fired units
would have “0-50% natural gas-burning capability.” The Kentucky commission’s staff report on
EKPC’s 2025 integrated resource plan records Spurlock’s coal-fired generation as totaling 1,346
MW. Commission Staff’s Report, App. A to Order, Case No. 2025-00087, at 26 & n.118 (Ky. PSC
June 1, 2026). Columbia Gulf’s own fuel study, filed as Attachment A on June 23, 2026 (Accession
No. 20260623-5110), applies a 75 percent load factor to the 340,000 Dth/d of certificated capacity.
Nothing in the EA relates the certificated capacity to the heat input of the units it is said to serve.




             Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 8
 Mr. Kulovsek requests that Columbia Gulf be directed to state on the record when, and on what
basis, the Project’s capacity increased from 140,000 Dth/d to 340,000 Dth/d.

C. The record contains evidence bearing on need that the EA does not address

The Commission may generally rely on a precedent agreement to establish market need, and the
D.C. Circuit has limited the exception recognized in Environmental Defense Fund v. FERC, 2
F.4th 953, 975 (D.C. Cir. 2021), to agreements between affiliated entities where there is plausible
evidence of self-dealing. Sierra Club v. FERC, No. 24-1099, slip op. (D.C. Cir. Sept. 30, 2025).
Columbia Gulf and EKPC are not affiliates, and Mr. Kulovsek does not allege self-dealing. He
raises the following record evidence for a different reason: the Commission acts arbitrarily when
it fails to respond to a specific challenge to its reliance on precedent agreements and discredits
contrary record evidence without explanation. New Jersey Conservation Foundation v. FERC, 111
F.4th 42 (D.C. Cir. 2024). The EA’s purpose-and-need statement is two sentences long and recites
the applicant’s position; it does not mention the fuel study, EPIC Report No. 2026-001, or any of
the following:

   •   EKPC told the Kentucky commission in Case No. 2024-00370 that “[t]he addition of gas
       pipelines, owned and operated by a pipeline company, with available capacity will only
       enhance the desirability of these locations” for economic development; that “EKPC’s
       known interest from data center investors on its system will exceed the size of our existing
       fleet alone by that time, more than doubling our load today”; and that “the 2024 Load
       Forecast does not specifically include any potential data center load.” Application at 6;
       Direct Testimony of Don Mosier at 7, 9.

   •   The Kentucky Energy Planning and Inventory Commission’s Report No. 2026-001 (June
       2026), filed as Exhibit A to the Fifth Supplemental, states at page 5 that “EKPC currently
       has 11 active data center projects seeking over 10 GW of power” and lists Mason County
       among the counties with projects under consideration.

   •   EKPC’s May 6, 2025 presentation to the PJM Transmission Expansion Advisory
       Committee describes a new customer in Mason County whose load ramps from 110 MW
       in December 2026 to 2,200 MW by January 2031, served in part by a new 345-kV double
       circuit from Spurlock Station. EKPC filed that presentation with the Kentucky commission




            Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 9
        on December 17, 2025 as its response to Staff’s First Data Request, Item 2, in Case No.
       2025-00311.

   •   The Kentucky Lantern reported on July 7, 2026 that “an undisclosed company looking to
       build a hyperscale data center in Mason County would use an enormous 1.2 gigawatts of
       electricity; the coal-fired Hugh. L. [sic] Spurlock Generating Station in that county can
       produce, at max capacity, roughly 1.3 gigawatts.” Liam Niemeyer, See where data center
       developers are looking to build in Kentucky, Kentucky Lantern (July 7, 2026).

   •   On August 4, 2026, the Mason County Attorney, John F. Estill, responding in writing to
       Mr. Kulovsek’s Kentucky Open Records Act request, stated that “[t]he data center prospect
       continues to conduct its due diligence for the possible development of a major project in
       Mason County,” and that “Mason County has enacted two ordinances adopting the
       recommendations of the Joint Planning Commission, regulating data centers in general,
       and amending the zoning map to permit data centers in a designated area of western Mason
       County.” The letter is filed as Exhibit E. The Kentucky Attorney General’s open records
       decision 25-ORD-265 (Sept. 19, 2025) records that Mason County officials are “currently
       under a nondisclosure agreement” with the prospect.

Mr. Kulovsek makes no representation about the identity of the prospect and does not ask the
Commission to analyze the effects of any data center. He asks the Commission to require Columbia
Gulf to state on the record what the 340,000 Dth/d of firm capacity is for: the identity of each firm
shipper and its share of capacity, the end use each shipper has represented, and whether any part
of the capacity is committed, directly or indirectly, to serve new electric generation added for large-
load industrial customers. Mr. Kulovsek does not ask the Commission to look behind the precedent
agreement. He asks that the need finding state, on the public record, how 340,000 Dth/d relates to
the fuel requirement of the units the Project is said to serve. At the 10,000 Btu/kWh average heat
rate recited in EKPC’s May 13, 2025 resolution, 1,346 MW of capacity operating at full load
would require approximately 323,000 Dth/d if fired entirely on natural gas, and approximately
161,000 Dth/d at the 50 percent co-firing maximum EKPC described to the Kentucky commission.
Either the certificated capacity exceeds the stated purpose or the purpose has changed; the record
should say which.




            Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 10
 D. The Pulaski Project is the related Columbia Gulf lateral, and the EA does not mention it

The Sixth Supplemental (Accession No. 20260721-5110) asked staff to address the relationship
between this Project and the NKY Gate Enhancement Project (Docket No. CP26-19-000). The EA
answers that the two projects “are unrelated and have different purposes and needs,” because the
NKY Gate project replaces 1950s-era infrastructure, and that “neither project would meet the
other’s purpose and need, and therefore would not be viable system alternatives.” EA at 60. Mr.
Kulovsek does not contest that answer for purposes of these comments.

The related project is a different one. The Amended and Restated Precedent Agreements approved
on May 13, 2025 cover two Columbia Gulf laterals for the same customer, both upsized to 30-inch
pipe by the same board action: the Spurlock lateral before this Commission, and the Cooper Station
lateral, which is Columbia Gulf’s Pulaski Project, Docket No. CP26-11-000. The Pulaski Project
is 41.3 miles of new 30-inch pipeline from Lincoln County to Pulaski County, Kentucky, serving
EKPC’s John S. Cooper Power Station; staff issued its environmental assessment for that project
on June 22, 2026, and its 90-day federal authorization deadline is September 20, 2026. 91 Fed.
Reg. 1306 (Jan. 13, 2026); 91 Fed. Reg. 38414 (June 25, 2026). The two projects share a sponsor,
a customer, a contractual program, a pipe diameter selected in a single board resolution, and a
stated purpose of supporting EKPC’s co-firing conversions. The Maysville EA does not mention
the Pulaski Project.

The Commission’s regulations require each resource report to “[i]dentify the effects of
construction, operation (including maintenance and malfunctions), and termination of the project,
as well as cumulative effects resulting from existing or reasonably foreseeable projects.” 18 C.F.R.
§ 380.12(b)(3). Mr. Kulovsek is aware that the Commission held in Eastern Gas Transmission and
Storage, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,218 (2026), that NEPA does not require a cumulative-effects analysis
as a separate category, and that the two laterals are geographically distinct. He does not ask for a
combined effects analysis. He asks that the Commission acknowledge on the record that the
Maysville and Pulaski laterals arise from a single set of amended precedent agreements and a
single upsizing decision, and that it address whether evaluating the need for each lateral in isolation
is consistent with its obligation under section 7 of the Natural Gas Act to determine whether this
Project, at this capacity, is required by the public convenience and necessity. See Delaware




            Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 11
 Riverkeeper Network v. FERC, 753 F.3d 1304, 1313 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (agency must address the
“true scope” of the activities under consideration).

E. The premise of the stated need has changed since the application was filed

EKPC’s stated reason for co-firing Spurlock was compliance with the Environmental Protection
Agency’s April 2024 greenhouse-gas rule for existing coal-fired units, which required 40 percent
natural gas co-firing by January 1, 2030 as the condition of continued operation. Direct Testimony
of Don Mosier, Case No. 2024-00370, at 3, 18; Order, Case No. 2024-00370, at 52-53 (Ky. PSC
July 3, 2025). Since Columbia Gulf filed its application, EPA has proposed to repeal those
standards, 90 Fed. Reg. 25752 (June 17, 2025), and on May 14, 2026 transmitted a final repeal
rule to the Office of Management and Budget for review; EPA has rescinded the 2009
endangerment finding, 91 Fed. Reg. 7686 (Feb. 18, 2026) (effective April 20, 2026); and EPA has
repealed the 2024 amendments to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards, 91 Fed. Reg. 9088 (Feb.
24, 2026). The EA describes the conversion only as “part of EKPC’s state approved initiative,”
EA at 1, without noting that the state approval rested on a federal compliance deadline that the
federal government has moved to eliminate.

Mr. Kulovsek does not ask the Commission to analyze EPA rulemaking or EKPC’s operating
decisions. He asks that the Commission’s finding on need address whether the applicant’s stated
purpose still rests on the premise on which it was presented, and that Columbia Gulf be directed
to state whether the precedent agreement contains any condition tied to the co-firing conversion
proceeding.

F. A federal district court has vacated the environmental review of a comparable coal-to-gas
project on grounds the parties have publicly described as bearing on Parts III.A through III.E

On August 31, 2026, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee entered
judgment in Appalachian Voices v. Tennessee Valley Authority, No. 3:24-cv-00411 (E.D. Tenn.),
a challenge under NEPA and the Administrative Procedure Act to TVA’s decision to retire coal-
fired units at its Kingston Fossil Plant and replace them with natural gas generation and associated
pipeline capacity. The order is under seal as of this filing. Mr. Kulovsek has not read it and does
not characterize its reasoning. He relies only on the following, each from a public source: news
reports describe TVA’s motion for a stay pending appeal as stating that the judgment “vacated
TVA’s Environmental Impact Statement and Record of Decision” for the project; the plaintiffs


              Docket No. CP26-25-000 | Tenth Supplemental Comments of Justin Kulovsek | Page 12
 describe the grounds as a failure to evaluate cleaner and less costly alternatives and the
commitment of ratepayer funds to the gas plant before the decision to build it was made; and TVA
has stated that it will appeal. Court ruling could halt construction of Kingston gas plant as TVA
appeals decision, WATE (Sept. 8, 2026); Center for Biological Diversity, Court Rules TVA’s
Decision to Build Kingston Gas Plant Broke Law (Sept. 8, 2026).

Two features of that record are pertinent here, and neither depends on the sealed opinion. First, the

D. Section 106 and tribal consultation

The EA states that Section 106 compliance “cannot be completed at this time” pending deep testing
at four archaeological sites and recommends Condition 17. EA at 42, 68. In the segment near
Sharon Sanders’ property at Mileposts 31.30 to 31.77, Columbia Gulf documented two sites,
15Ms280 and 15Ms290; the Kentucky SHPO concurred on February 10, 2026 that the portion of
15Ms290 within the area of potential effect is not eligible, and deep testing at 15Ms280 remains
incomplete, with the addendum report not anticipated until November 2026. Motion of Sharon
Sanders, Accession No. 20260803-5160; EA at 10, 40-41. Under 36 C.F.R. § 800.1(c) the Section
106 process must be completed prior to the issuance of a license. The EA also records that the
Cherokee Nation requested government-to-government consultation and copies of the survey
reports on November 13, 2025, and that the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma was sent a
notification letter on April 15, 2026, but does not state whether the Cherokee Nation’s request has
been honored or whether the survey reports have been provided. EA at 41. Mr. Kulovsek does not
speak for any Tribe. He requests only that staff confirm the status of both matters on the record
and confirm that no certificate order will issue before Section 106 consultation is complete or, if
the Commission intends to proceed on a conditioned order, that it explain how that course satisfies
§ 800.1(c).

E. The county governments’ filed opposition

Rowan County Fiscal Court filed Resolution No. 08-25, adopted August 19, 2025, opposing the
Project (Accession No. 20260514-5070). Fleming County Fiscal Court filed comments and a
resolution in opposition (Accession No. 20260514-5030); its late motion to intervene was denied
on June 1, 2026, and the Commission stated that it “will consider the comments included in the
Fleming County Fiscal Court’s May 14, 2026 filing” (Accession No. 20260601-3023 & n.3). The
EA acknowledges receipt of comments from both fiscal courts. EA at 4. It does not address their
substance: county road use and maintenance during construction, floodplain administration, and
the capacity of county emergency services, all of which are governmental functions no individual

 landowner represents. Mr. Kulovsek requests that any order address the counties’ filed comments
on the record.

F. Emergency-response coordination has not been documented

The EA acknowledges that commenters “expressed concern about the ability of rural, volunteer-
based emergency services to respond to a pipeline incident” and “asked whether site-specific
emergency coordination had occurred, and whether the operator would train local responders.” EA
at 57. Its answer describes the requirements of 49 C.F.R. § 192.615 in general terms and states that
“Columbia Gulf would provide the appropriate training to local emergency service personnel
before the facilities are placed in service.” Id. The EA does not state whether liaison under §
192.615(c) has occurred with any fire department, emergency medical service, 9-1-1 center, or
county emergency management director in Rowan, Fleming, or Mason County. Mr. Kulovsek
requests that Columbia Gulf be directed to file, before any order issues, a statement identifying
each such organization by county, the date liaison occurred or is scheduled, and the training it will
provide.

G. Public participation

The Commission cancelled the in-person scoping sessions on January 23, 2026 because of a winter
storm (Accession No. 20260123-3045) and substituted a single virtual session on February 19,
2026. The EA reports that “[t]wo individuals attended the virtual comment session,” that “[w]e
received numerous comments requesting a new meeting following cancellation of the in-person
scoping session,” and that a commenter noted “there was no comment session in Rowan County.”
EA at 4 & n.3. No Commission-sponsored in-person session was ever held in any of the three
counties. The Notice of Schedule stated that “[a]ll substantive comments will be addressed in the
EA.” 91 Fed. Reg. 2338 (Jan. 20, 2026). The EA does not address the fuel study, the capacity
record, the property-access record, or the measurement-methodology comments in Mr. Kulovsek’s
filings; the terms “fuel study,” “data center,” and “cumulative” do not appear in it. Mr. Kulovsek
requests that the Commission reopen the comment period for a period of not less than 30 days once
the Section 404 verification, the completed Endangered Species Act consultation, the Phase 1
mussel survey results, and the Section 106 determinations are filed on the docket, so that those
documents and Water Quality Certification WQC2026-058-7 (Accession No. 20260909-5124)
may be addressed together.

 VII. DOCUMENTARY ERRORS IN THE EA

Staff’s certification states that “the analysis contained within this environmental document is an
accurate representation of the potential environmental effects of the proposed action and the
analysis is substantially complete.” The following errors, each verifiable from the face of the
document, should be corrected in any supplemental document or order:

   •   The EA states that “Kentucky has formally adopted executive or legislative statewide goals
       for GHG emissions reduction targets.” EA at 48. Kentucky has adopted no such target. The
       sentence does not describe Kentucky and should be corrected.

   •   The EA states that FERC “contacted the tribes by letter on March 5, 2025.” EA at 41. The
       letters were issued March 5, 2026 (Accession Nos. 20260305-3032 through 20260305-
       3038), more than three months after the application was filed.

   •   The EA describes the non-jurisdictional facility as “EKPC’s New Hugh L. Spurlock Station
       1360-MW Generating Unit in Mason County, as discussed in section A.8.” EA at 12.
       Section A.8 is the construction schedule; the non-jurisdictional facilities are in section A.6,
       and the EA’s own purpose-and-need statement describes the conversion of “all four of the
       existing coal units,” not a new unit. EA at 1, 6. The Kentucky commission’s staff report
       puts Spurlock’s coal-fired capacity at 1,346 MW.

   •   The subtotal and total rows of Table B-1 do not sum from the line items shown. The Project
       Total row reports 5.23 tons of sulfur dioxide although every sulfur dioxide line item in the
       table is 0.00, and reports 5.04 tons of PM2.5, which equals the Mason County subtotal
       alone. EA at 44-45.

   •   The EA cites “Richards, 2026” for the remediation status of the Maxey Flats site, EA at
       18, and “EPA, 2026a; 2026b” for the status of the remediation wells near Milepost 37.7,
       EA at 19; neither appears in Appendix B.

   •   The construction schedule states that construction “would commence as early as February
       2027,” that “[c]learing and grading would begin around March 2028,” and that facilities
       would be placed in service by February 2029, while the non-jurisdictional conversion the
       Project serves is not expected to reach commercial operation until December 2029. EA at
       6-7.

wetlands found to be unsaturated at the time of construction will be similar to those used in upland
areas. In saturated wetlands where soils are unstable, temporary work surfaces of timber or travel
pads will be installed. Construction will proceed in saturated wetlands, except topsoil will not be
segregated due to the saturated, unconsolidated conditions.

will not be maintained in order to avoid and minimize impacts on wetlands. Following the

We received two public comments from a Justin Kulovsek raising concerns with groundwater pollution, karst geology
aquatic transfer, and radioactive material from Maxey Flats. After speaking with groundwater and the manager of
Maxey Flats, the issues raised by the commenter are important, but unfortunately fall outside of our regulatory

Justin responded to our clarifications to these issues on 7/6/2026.



“Thank you for the July 2 response addressing my comments on the Maysville Project certification. I appreciate the
Division taking the time to review them and the invitation to keep participating in the comment process. I want to
accept one point, clarify a second, and refocus my concerns in a way I hope is squarely within the Division's
authority.



First, I accept that a 401 certification decision rests on Kentucky's water quality standards, and that those standards
under 401 KAR Chapter 10 are written for surface waters. I am not asking the Division to certify or deny based on
groundwater standards that do not exist.



Second, one clarification for the record. The response states that groundwater is not a water of the Commonwealth
under KRS 224.1-010. That statute actually defines “waters of the Commonwealth” to include wells, springs, and all
other bodies of water, surface and underground. Groundwater is within the definition. I understand the operative

point is the absence of groundwater water quality standards, not the definition, and I raise this only so the record is
accurate.



Third, and most important, my central concern is a surface water concern, and I do not believe it was reached in the
response. Kentucky's own water quality standards define “surface waters” to include “any subterranean waters
flowing in well-defined channels and having a demonstrable hydrologic connection with the surface” (401 KAR
10:001, Section 1(72)). Karst conduits and the springs they feed are exactly that. Columbia Gulf's Resource Report 2
states that contamination “is capable of being rapidly transmitted to and discharged from the Silurian-Devonian
aquifer to wells and springs.” Those springs discharge to streams. Sediment, trench dewatering water, hydrostatic
test water, or a spill that travels through karst to a spring or stream is a surface water impact. The project also open-
cuts and directionally drills jurisdictional streams, including the North Fork Licking River.”

construction sampling of springs and streams within the karst corridor for degradation accountability, and a written
and researched contingency plan for stream crossings and karst features.

issuance of securities or indebtedness is payable at periods of not more than two years

initial issuance date.
